en: Now begins the Lamp of Yoga (Yogapradīpa):
As long as you are not devoured by diseases, as long as old age does not approach you, and as long as your vital breath has not failed, perform what is auspicious. 1.
One should reflect upon oneself: "From where have I come? Where will I go? Whence have I arrived at this moment? Who is my kinsman? To whom do I belong?"
Two kinds of men desire sacred fords; what is the use of those fords that are causes of affliction?
The ford of Dharma residing within the body is considered superior to all other fords.
Those who wander about thinking, "This is a sacred ford, this is a sacred ford," while being devoid of knowledge and meditation, find that their own self is indeed the true sacred ford.
Remaining in this body, one may consume everything acquired from birth;
yet no one sees this self at all, for Hara (Śiva) destroys it for one who beholds it.
The world regards even a petty thief as a robber of all one's possessions when he has taken even a small object;
yet fools do not perceive themselves as such, even when they have taken everything.
Therefore, even in that state, when and by what means should yogis always observe their own self, which has taken refuge in the fortress of the body and is shrouded by ignorance? 6–7.
In this world, the self itself when well-pleased is proclaimed to be a happy rebirth;
conversely, when it is displeased, this will undoubtedly result in an unhappy rebirth.
He who, out of a desire for his vision, visits sacred ford after sacred ford here in this world— yet that very deity cannot be seen while remaining within this very body.
Wandering here from place to place for the sake of beholding the gods, those of ignorant intellect do not see the God who resides within their own bodies. 10.
10–11. Liberated from all realms, having the nature of gnosis, stainless,
and indeed free from karma— the Self alone should be meditated upon by those desiring liberation.
Immersed in the nectar of contentment, always equal toward enemy and friend, indifferent to pleasure and pain, and turned away from passion and hatred. ||12||
The Lord, one's own Self, should be established as glorious like a mass of light, the benefactor of the entire universe, ever full with the bliss of eternal joy. 13.
Resembling pure crystal, adorned with the qualities of omniscience, and endowed with the digits of the Supreme Self— thus should one’s own self be meditated upon by the wise. 14.

14–15. However, having abandoned everything such as the seats (pīṭha) and so forth, which consist of the six wheels, those seeking liberation must meditate upon this very Self alone in a meditation devoid of form.
In this way, through the practice of yoga and by means of this meditation, the yogis perceive their own self as it truly exists, situated within the body.
16–17. He by whom the Puruṣa, who is devoid of qualities and primordial nature (prakṛti), has not been known— by him alone should pilgrimages, sacrifices, and the like be practiced, and not by yogis.
Knowledge of the Self is the supreme sacred ford; water is not called a sacred ford.
That purification which comes through knowledge of one's own Self is remembered as the highest purification.
Knowledge of the Self is the supreme dharma; it is the foremost of all dharmas and ritual acts. For from that, immortality is attained by all who possess true knowledge. 18
Without self-knowledge, liberation cannot be attained even by yogis, despite their having performed difficult austerities and various pure vows. 18–20a.
Consisting of all phenomena, glorious, and free from all [notions of] gold, this self is known by him; thus his birth exists. 21
Having thus meditated upon one's own self as being devoid of a body within one's own body,
one should meditate upon the Lord of Gods, who has ascended to the supreme state, for the sake of liberation.
Whether it be Śaṅkara or the Lord of Jinas, whoever is always one's preferred deity,
that single Lord alone is seen as peaceful and established in nirvāṇa.
Worshipped by the lords of gods, asuras, and men, he who is the benefactor of the worlds and liberated from all defects is proclaimed as the Lord of Devas. 24.
Transcending the paths of merit and demerit, the destroyer of the creeper of existence,
unmanifest yet possessing manifest form, he is all-knowing and all-seeing.
Formless, without appearance, free from conceptual proliferation, and stainless,
the Lord is eternally composed of bliss; he is the perfected one, the awakened one, and free from all affliction.
He is infinite and absolute, eternal, of the nature of space, and everlasting; the God above all gods, the soul of the universe, pervading all, and ancient. ||27||
Transcending the entire range of karma, he is both with parts and without parts;
he is the Supreme Self, the supreme light, the supreme Brahman, higher than the highest.
Free from the three qualities (guṇas), devoid of smell and touch,
he is neither to be cut nor to be pierced; he is untainted, stainless, and the sovereign Lord.

He possesses attributes yet is devoid of attributes; he is peaceful, the savior from the ocean of worldly existence; difficult to perceive, yet he has become the object of perception; he is golden-hued, yet free from all color.
Though he is one, he appears in many forms; he is gross and subtle, light and heavy; having ascended to the state of Nirvāṇa, he is here called the Lord of Gods (Deveśa). ||31||
Brahmā is perceived by the Brahmins, and Viṣṇu likewise by the best of those who wear yellow robes;
Rudra is seen by the ascetics— it is this very one who is stainless.
He is called Jinendra by the Jains, and having made him Buddha, he is called by the Buddhists; by the Kaulikas he is declared as Kola—this very one is the eternal [Lord]. 33.
Just as a crystal may appear in many forms when it is free from adjuncts, so too, though it is one, it is known as manifold through the six modes of perception.
Just as water may appear in many forms due to the differences in the colors of the earth [upon which it rests],
so too is He proclaimed to be of manifold forms through the diversity of phenomenal states.
Because of the differences in their dispositions, philosophical systems do not stand upon a single path;
even when they converge on a single objective, these five remain distinct, just like the five sense objects.
Partless, free from the sense of "mine," peaceful, omniscient, the giver of bliss, and the Lord— he alone is the Blessed One, the one God to be known, the stainless one. 37.
The Lord of the World has the nature of space; he transcends action, time, and qualities; he is liberated from the creations of saṃsāra and is distinct from all radiance. 38.37–38.38
This Lord of Gods is said here to be complete with absolute knowledge (kevalajñāna), established in absolute bliss (kevalānanda), and attainable through absolute meditation (kevaladhyāna). 38–39.
Thus, one should meditate upon the Lord of Gods, who is filled with infinite virtues, who possesses infinite bliss, who has ascended to the state of liberation, and from whom there is no rebirth.
The yogi should bathe the Lord with the water of the Gaṅgā, which is naturally pure and red with tranquility, and then worship Him with fragrant flowers. 41.
In a vast place of devotion, having made the mind steady and focused,
one should pour forth the nectar and other offerings consisting of a flood of love and supreme bliss.
Having awakened the brilliantly blazing row of lamps with the splendor of wisdom, one should perform the ritual waving of lights (ārātrika) for the Lord's merit in due order. 43.
43–44. One should always think with devotion: "May I become a performer of worship for the Lord of Gods, the Sovereign, according to this very rule."
One should unite one's own self, the inner swan whose nature is consciousness, with the Supreme Self;
by uniting it with the supreme swan, one attains the state of Nirvana.
Then, having established one [of the two] through auspicious meditation, the knower of yoga should contemplate his own self as being of the nature of that Supreme Self. ||43||
I am the Supreme Self, whose nature is the sun of absolute knowledge (kevalajñāna); having abandoned the ocean of worldly existence, I have become one who has attained the empire of bliss. 43.47
"I am the stainless God, residing at the summit of all worlds"— one should always meditate upon this as the meditation that is the cause for the state of imperishability. 48.
When the self is absorbed in meditation, the sign observed in the stainless deity is that tears of bliss flow and the hair stands on end. ||49||

Restraint (saṃyama), observance (niyama), and the third, the instrument (karaṇa); breath control (prāṇāyāma), withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), concentration (samādhi), and likewise meditative fixation (dhāraṇā).
Thus, meditation is to be known here by the wise as the eightfold limb of yoga;
when performed with all its limbs complete, this leads to liberation for the virtuous.
That is the Dharma, that is the quality, that is the vow, that is the meditation, and that indeed is the yoga;
for that alone is the ascent to the state where the mind is not afflicted.
Free from conceptualization and discursive thought, devoid of causal factors, one who is intent upon the object of meditation and the act of holding it dwells in that eternal, stainless state. ||53||
One should always yoke the mind to its own true nature and practice meditation upon that state; the yogi who has reached that level shall not undergo birth again. 54
The object of knowledge transcends all states; knowledge is said to be the mind.
One should make knowledge and the object of knowledge equal; there is no other path to liberation.
Having led the mind above the eyebrows, that which is beyond is beheld; it is higher than the high, subtle, and stainless. [It is subtle.]
Liberation exists through the former path, yet it is not found in the latter;
in the state of Unmanī, which is beyond paths, liberation occurs even without a path.

Through the abandonment of the delusion of existence, one who abides in the innate state (sahaja), whose nature is the single flavor of bliss, is said to be on the path of liberation for the virtuous. ||58||
The mind which is devoid of the body, free from inhalation and exhalation, beyond the path of coming and going, and devoid of all activity.
Without support, without foundation, the support of all, of great manifestation,
and transcendent— that stainless state is to be known by yogis.
Where the breath ceases and where the mind dissolves— that subtle, undecaying, and immortal state is to be known as the innate abode.
Through the constant practice of yoga, the mind, being liberated from its mental activities,
attains the state of *unmanī* (the transmental) and gradually reaches that supreme state.
When the mind, its attachment to sense objects liberated, becomes completely stilled within the heart and reaches the state of non-thought, that is the supreme state.
When the meditator, the meditation, and the object of meditation become non-dual through the absence of fear, one reaches that state;
this is the state of equal flavor (samarasībhāva), which is considered the unification [of all].
Now, therefore, the reality of that subtle, formless, and auspicious meditation is being declared; it is difficult to know even for the great. 64–65.
65–66. While sleeping at night, a certain mute person here obtained a dream;
yet because he is mute, he does not speak even of the dream, and therefore the dream is not understood by him.
66–67. O gentle one, listen now with reverence to who that mute was, what kind of night it was, and what the fruit of even his dream was for the wise woman.
When the yogi, mute and with his mind asleep in the night of ignorance, experiences a dream composed of objective phenomena, it brings him joy. (67–68)
By that yogin, a firm disposition has been established in the Supreme Brahman;
his disposition, being directed toward the Supreme Brahman, shall result in the fruit of liberation.
The mind that has transcended both the moon and the sun, is devoid of the movement of breath, and is free from conceptual construction, is said to be the Supreme Brahman.

That which is to be known as the Supreme Brahman itself must always be understood by the wise for the sake of perfection; O wise one, I have explained the meaning of dreams before you through the application of yoga.
One should not think of anything at all; the mind conjoined with the state beyond mind (unmanībhāva), formless and exceedingly subtle— that is called the great meditation (mahādhyāna).

The divisions of this [meditator] that were previously described as the white dhyānas consist of seventy-two words in the form of *piṇḍas*; for the sake of his ascent, they are like the word-based [verses] in a temple. ||72||
"What am I like? Where shall I go? What do I do? What do I remember?"—thus the yogin knows nothing when merged in the stainless state of dissolution.
When the eye of knowledge is covered by sense objects, which are like cataracts,
living beings do not see the door to the city of perfection, which is meditative concentration.
When the five flickering, desirable sense-objects, each with its own name,
are not restrained by the senses, the mind turns away from meditation.
When those impurities and the sense-faculties have been brought to tranquility,
and steadiness in meditation has been achieved, the mind should be made free from volitional constructions.
Meditation joined with the mind— by whomsoever that mind, whether moving or unmoving, has been brought under control, for them the three worlds shall become subject.
Whatever wholesome action one performs, one should perform it together with the mind,
because the fruit is equal to the mind; furthermore, in emptiness, it becomes empty again.
Just as an archer who has practiced becomes single-minded and, with focused attention, pierces the target,
so too the yogi accomplishes his desired task through one-pointedness of mind.
Therefore, one should cultivate a mind that is the most excellent essence, pure, the destroyer of karma, the supreme among all dharmas, and whose nature is the flavor of tranquility.

Even that which has been accumulated over eighty lakhs of births through fierce vows may, in some instance, be exhausted in an instant by that mind which is immersed in the essence of tranquility. 81.
81–82. Through the renunciation of all undertakings, when the mind has attained the flavor of tranquility,
that is the perfection for the virtuous which serves as the means for bathing in all sacred fords.
While the supreme Yoga, whose nature is the state of equal flavor (samarasa), exists, the deluded,
though practicing yoga after yoga, wander aimlessly in every direction.
There is a distinction of caste only so long as one does not attain Brahman;
once they have reached the supreme Brahman, all castes are twice-born.
There are eighty-four dense paths of dharma that differentiate various views;
for the sake of liberation, they reach a state of equality, just as rivers flow into the ocean. [They go?]
Just as the milk of cows of many different colors is of a single color, so too is the path to liberation the same for all six paths of vision. 86.
The mind that is free from conceptualization and imagination, always devoid of attachment and aversion, and merged in the dissolution of eternal bliss, is known as the state of equanimity (samarasa).
That mind which does not grieve over the past or the future is called *sāmāyika*; it is like a lamp situated in a windless place.
That mind which is free from attachment, devoid of appearances, without rejection, without support, and liberated from merit and demerit, is known as *sāmāyika*.
When there is no sorrow at departure and no joy at arrival, and the mind regards enemy and friend as equal—this is called equanimity (sāmāyika) here. 90.
Whatever treatise spreads throughout this world that has been composed by bad poets is designated as ignorance; it is a state of equality that causes delusion.
Just as deluded beings do not see forms at night in the darkness, so too those shrouded by the darkness of ignorance do not perceive reality.
92-93. This wicked ignorance, consisting of delusion and illusion, was created on earth as a constant bolt barring the path to liberation for the virtuous who desire emancipation.
Knowing this thus, the wise, always desiring their own welfare,
have [striven] against ignorance on this earth.
Knowing this, the wise should always avoid it from afar and never listen to it at any time. 94.94
But the true knowledge spoken by the Omniscient One is the cause for severing cyclic existence;
that alone should always be cultivated by the virtuous, as it bestows the path to liberation. (95)
Sattva, rajas, and tamas—these are the three qualities within the body; having abandoned both rajas and tamas, one should take refuge in sattva alone. (96)
Sattva is the support of all virtues; sattva is that which upholds the Dharma; sattva is the destroyer of saṃsāra; sattva is that which bestows heaven and liberation. ||97||
In the auspicious palace consisting of meditation— which is without support, without form, eternally blissful, and motionless— the firm pillar of sattva is considered to be established. (98)
Just as masses of wood are consumed even by a small spark of fire,
so too are the karmas of yogis exhausted by means of pure meditation (śukladhyāna).
How could the dust and impurity of karma remain for even a single moment in that great water, pure through meditation, where the lord of yogis constantly bathes?
Just as water does not naturally cling to the petals of a lotus, nor does a stone situated in the midst of water ever break apart. (102)
Just as a crystal would not become soiled when covered by dust, so the self, relying upon right meditation, is not defiled by sins. (103)
The yogi who is united with the pure meditation, who knows Brahman and is established in Brahman,
attains the supreme fruit at the very tip of the branch, even while remaining on the ground.
Through this meditation on the supreme bliss of the glory of liberation, the yogi should then constantly practice the formless meditation that transcends all forms.

Having repeatedly studied the meaning of reality from the scriptures, the wise person, for the sake of the knowledge of reality, should finally discard the scriptures entirely, just as one discards straw. (106)
What is to be gained by those syllables which perish with time? As long as one has not attained the Imperishable, how can there be the bliss of liberation? (107)
Meditation is a wish-fulfilling tree in this world; it is perpetually in bloom with the flowers of wisdom and bears the fruits of the nectar of liberation that bestow happiness. (108)
Act in such a way that the wise man, taking refuge in the tree of pure meditation and gathering the flowers of knowledge, may obtain the fruit of liberation.
In this very life, O gentle one, the eternal yogi, having become of the nature of space through pure meditation and being forever blissful, shall go to the state of liberation.
Yoga, consisting of the three jewels in the form of knowledge, vision, and conduct, is proclaimed as the means for attaining the state of liberation. ||111||
That yoga, which brings about liberation by severing the activity of saṃsāra,
is further divided into eight types according to its constituent limbs beginning with *saṃyama*. ||112||
Furthermore, gems, fire, stars, the moon, the sun, and so forth,
also stimulate only a small portion of the external earth-element here.
The light arising from the dissolution into the innate (sahaja) always illumines the three worlds within, including all distinctions between the subtle and the gross.
One should meditate upon the unstruck sound (anāhatanāda), which is the vibration of supreme bliss, subtle, the ultimate object of focus through one's own experience, located below the dvādaśānta.
He who knows that dissolution of the sound of *praṇava*, which is like a continuous stream of oil, covered by the resonance of a long bell, is a knower of yoga.
Just as when the sound of a bell has subsided, it becomes sweet even though it is unstruck; so too should the meaning be contemplated as peaceful, even when the sound has ceased. (117)
Abiding in the hearts of all beings, that sound resonates in an unmanifest form;
therefore, that sound is called "unstruck" (anāhata), for it is not a sound produced by manifest articulation.
It does not abide within the entire body, nor is it situated at the tip of the nose; though present before all beings, it is seen yet cannot be perceived.
That mind which is free from the resonance of syllables, waveless, and established in equanimity—abiding in the state of the co-emergent (*sahaja*)—is *nāda*; by that, [the world] is differentiated.
The senses remain only so long, and the passions indeed persist only so long, as the mind of the yogin has not dissolved into the unstruck sound (anāhata-nāda).

Sensual pleasure appears delightful only so long as the bliss arising from the unstruck sound (*anāhata*) has not been attained by the yogi through this meditation on the karma accumulated at the time of birth.
All that perishes in an instant, like darkness at the rising of the sun. Thus,
it is clear that both the gross and the subtle, as well as the formal, constitute auspicious meditation.
That which transcends form has been fully described; now the formless is being spoken of.
Even the formless meditation is radiant and transcends form.
It is proclaimed to be of two kinds, distinguished as gross and subtle.
Having abandoned the entire body, the mind remains steady at the aperture of Brahma (brahmadvāra).
If that is performed, it is here called subtle and formless; indeed,
through the practice of constant repetition in the pure, unstruck state of meditation.
The yogi should establish the mind in union with the formless state at the *dvādaśānta*,
having abandoned both the external and internal Brahman as well as the conditioned self.
One should take refuge in the door of Brahman, which is formless, the station of the Supreme Self,
measuring one finger-breadth in size, perfectly circular, and resembling the sky. ||128||128||
The lord of yogins should first contemplate [the breath] as far as the *dvādaśānta*;
established there, he is called the twelve-fold one (*dvādaśātmā*), the auspicious eye.
Therefore, the Brahman situated even above that is likewise remembered as being at the end of the twelve;
it transcends sound, the point, and the digit, and is endowed with the digit of the Supreme Self.
The yogi, having restrained the flow of the passions and having controlled his own extremely fickle senses, should always meditate upon the *dvādaśānta*, the sole abode of eternal bliss.
Having abandoned attachment to anything else and fixed his intellect on the attainment of the bliss of the supreme state,

he should make his own mind steady, firmly rely upon a nature imbued with the essence of tranquility, and— remaining untainted by the disputes of impure doctrines— he should strive daily to meditate on the stainless meditation. 132
Having severed the bonds of cyclic existence and conquered the internal forces such as delusion, that wise man, exerting himself, attained the initiation that grants liberation from the Lord Pārśva.
Having produced this pure knowledge through absorption in the realization of Brahman,
he attained the state of liberation which is eternally composed of bliss, his eightfold karma having been exhausted.
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-attachment—these are the vows; here, restraint is said to be fivefold. ||134||
Purity, austerity, contentment, self-study, and remembrance of the deity—these are to be known as the fivefold observances (niyama). Furthermore, the means (karaṇa) is posture (āsana).
Furthermore, steadiness in inhalation and exhalation is breath control (prāṇāyāma);
withdrawal (pratyāhāra) is the destruction of the objects of the senses, which is concentration (samāhita).
Concentration (*samādhi*) is the contemplation of the meaning of words;
for the sake of stability, people whose wealth consists of meditative retention (*dhāraṇā*) should have this as their object of meditation.
Whether it be gross or subtle, with form or formless, one should practice meditation with a steady mind focused upon a single object of perception. (138)
Thus, yoga is constituted by the eightfold methods, such as restraint (saṃyama) and the rest; meditation, endowed with all extraordinary powers, is the cause of auspiciousness. (139)
Salutation to that Self of all, who is the pervasive Lord in heaven, on earth, as well as in space; who shines both externally and internally, and whose very nature is light.
He who possesses the certainty that "I am neither bound nor liberated," and no other knowledge than that, is a fool; he alone has the qualification for this scripture. (141)
That which has renounced all conceptual constructions, whose sole wealth is latent impression (*vāsanā*), and whose form is the contemplation of "nothingness"—that is Brahman, the supreme state.
Thus ends the *Śrī Yogapradīpa*. This manuscript belongs to Harilāla.
Thus ends the book titled Śrī Yogapradīpa, belonging to Harilalya.
